newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary says Q2 energy price rise 3.3 pct at most.
newsitem.headline: Hungary says Q2 energy price rise 3.3 pct at most.

text.p: Hungary said on Tuesday demands by Western energy investors for more costs to be included in the country's quarterly adjustment to retail energy prices would not be met, meaning a probable July 1 price rise of no more than 3.3 percent.
"You can only count on 3.3 percent (for July 1)," Hungarian Energy Office (MEH) vice president Bela Nemeth told Reuters.

The MEH announced a 3.6 percent rise for April 1 which only took into account the devaluation of the forint in the first three months of the year and none of the other costs that outside investors have sought.

Western utilities such as Electricite de France (EdF) and German giant RWE, which have large stakes in Hungary's energy distribution companies, have been pushing since January for costs such as environmental safeguards, insurance and depreciation to be included in the government's energy pricing formula.
The July figure of 3.3 percent is based on the central bank crawling-peg devaluation rate for the forint, which was reduced on April 1 to 1.1 percent from 1.2 percent.
Pierre Abou, EdF representative in Hungary, told Reuters earlier that if no solution was found by the end of June, EdF would reconsider its position on future investments.
"If agreement is not reached before June we shall give them our precise standpoint," he said. "It is in our common interest to have this problem solved by the end of the quarter."
Nemeth said that the inclusion of any new costs such as environmental improvements in the new formula depended on a new legal framework being put in place.

"I hope it isn't (ready by June)...the time would be too short," he said, adding that agreement was unlikely before the end of 1997. "With the environmental costs, maybe the end of this year or next year."

In addition to EdF and RWE, other major Western utilities such as Gaz de France and Tractabel bought large stakes in the energy distribution sector at the end of 1995 and were promised an eight percent return on investment.

But they believe the government contravened the original sales agreements by cancelling planned price rises in last October and by fixing January energy price rises that still did not secure the expected margins.
"We are continuing not to get the promised profit," said Abou.
